## Facebook Use Predicts Declines in Subjective Well-Being in Young Adults

Ethan Kross 1 * , Philippe Verduyn 2 , Emre Demiralp 1 , Jiyoung Park 1 , David Seungjae Lee 1 , Natalie Lin 1 , Holly Shablack 1 , John Jonides 1 , Oscar Ybarra 1

1 Psychology Department, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America, 2 Psychology Department, University of Leuven, Leuven, Belgium

## Abstract

Over 500 million people interact daily with Facebook. Yet, whether Facebook use influences subjective well-being over time is unknown. We addressed this issue using experience-sampling, the most reliable method for measuring in-vivo behavior and psychological experience. We text-messaged people five times per day for two-weeks to examine how Facebook use influences the two components of subjective well-being: how people feel moment-to-moment and how satisfied they are with their lives. Our results indicate that Facebook use predicts negative shifts on both of these variables over time. The more people used Facebook at one time point, the worse they felt the next time we text-messaged them; the more they used Facebook over two-weeks, the more their life satisfaction levels declined over time. Interacting with other people ''directly'' did not predict these negative outcomes. They were also not moderated by the size of people's Facebook networks, their perceived supportiveness, motivation for using Facebook, gender, loneliness, self-esteem, or depression. On the surface, Facebook provides an invaluable resource for fulfilling the basic human need for social connection. Rather than enhancing well-being, however, these findings suggest that Facebook may undermine it.

Citation: Kross E, Verduyn P, Demiralp E, Park J, Lee DS, et al. (2013) Facebook Use Predicts Declines in Subjective Well-Being in Young Adults. PLoS ONE 8(8): e69841. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0069841

Editor: Ce ´ dric Sueur, Institut Pluridisciplinaire Hubert Curien, France

Received January 31, 2013; Accepted June 12, 2013; Published August 14, 2013

Funding: The authors have no support or funding to report.

Competing Interests: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.

* E-mail: ekross@umich.edu

## Introduction

Online social networks are rapidly changing the way human beings interact. Over a billion people belong to Facebook, the world's largest online social network, and over half of them log in daily [1]. Yet, no research has examined how interacting with Facebook influences subjective well-being over time. Indeed, a recent article that examined every peer-reviewed publication and conference proceeding on Facebook between 1/2005 and 1/2012 (412 in total) did not reveal a single study that examined how using this technology influences subjective well-being over time (Text S1) [2].

Subjective well-being is one of the most highly studied variables in the behavioral sciences. Although significant in its own right, it also predicts a range of consequential benefits including enhanced health and longevity [3-5]. Given the frequency of Facebook usage, identifying how interacting with this technology influences subjective well-being represents a basic research challenge that has important practical implications.

This issue is particularly vexing because prior research provides mixed clues about how Facebook use should influence subjective well-being. Whereas some cross-sectional research reveals positive associations between online social network use (in particular Facebook) and well-being [6], other work reveals the opposite [7,8]. headline.statement: The abstract states as a finding that the Facebook effects were "not moderated by" seven named variables, but not one coefficient, standard error, test statistic or exact p-value for any of roughly twelve moderation tests appears in the article or in any of its six supplements -- and Text S6, cited at exactly that point, is a single sentence explaining why one variable was not tested.
headline.evidence: Abstract: "They were also not moderated by the size of people's Facebook networks, their perceived supportiveness, motivation for using Facebook, gender, loneliness, self-esteem, or depression." Results, Moderation: "...interacted with Facebook use to predict changes in affective or cognitive well-being (Text S6). In no case did we observe any significant interactions ( p s . .16)." The entire contents of Text S6, read directly: "Text S6: 98% of participants reported using Facebook to 'keep in touch with friends.' Therefore, we did not test for moderation with this variable."
headline.plain: The paper's summary tells readers that the Facebook effect held regardless of things like gender, self-esteem, loneliness and depression. But the only evidence offered for that is the phrase "all p-values were above .16" -- no actual numbers for any of the roughly twelve tests involved, anywhere in the paper or its supporting files. The supporting file the authors point to at that exact sentence turns out to contain one sentence about a different matter entirely. With about 77 participants, a study like this has a weak ability to detect such patterns in the first place, so "we did not find it" is a long way from "it is not there", and a reader has no way to judge which of the two they are being told.

findings.title: Abstract's no-moderation claim rests on twelve tests for which no statistic is reported anywhere, and the supplement cited for them contains none
findings.reported: Abstract: "They were also not moderated by the size of people's Facebook networks, their perceived supportiveness, motivation for using Facebook, gender, loneliness, self-esteem, or depression." Results: "...participants' number of Facebook Friends, their perceptions of their Facebook network support, depressive symptoms, loneliness, gender, self-esteem, time of study participation, and motivation for using Facebook (e.g., to find new friends, to share good or bad things, to obtain new information) interacted with Facebook use to predict changes in affective or cognitive well-being (Text S6). In no case did we observe any significant interactions ( p s . .16)."
findings.computed: Twelve moderators are named; zero test statistics, coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals or exact p-values are reported for any of them, in the article or in any of the six supplements. Text S6, read directly at this stage via extract_supplement, is one sentence long and reports no moderation result: "98% of participants reported using Facebook to 'keep in touch with friends.' Therefore, we did not test for moderation with this variable." absence_of_evidence -- the check that would bound the largest moderating effect still compatible with these data -- could not be run at all, because it requires either a confidence interval or a coefficient with its standard error, and the paper prints neither for any moderation test.
findings.assumptions: The analytic n of about 77 is inferred from the paper's own residual degrees of freedom (73 with 3 predictors, 72 with 4, 71 with 5); the paper never prints a participant-level n. I did not derive standard errors from the printed coefficients, which would have been unguarded arithmetic. The judgement that low power makes the null uninformative is a statistical-power argument, not a tool result.

consequence.explanation: One of the four result sentences in the abstract asserts an absence of moderation across seven named variables that the published statistics cannot bound in either direction.

findings.plain: "We did not find a difference" is not the same as "there is no difference", and only the second of those can be stated as a finding. The abstract states the second. The support offered is a single phrase -- that every p-value was above .16 -- with no underlying numbers for any of the roughly twelve tests, and the supporting file the authors direct readers to at that sentence contains nothing about them. Because no margin of error is printed for any of these tests, neither a reader nor this analysis can work out how large a moderating effect would still be compatible with the data. The finding is about what can be checked, not about whether the authors' conclusion is wrong; it may well be right, but the paper does not let anyone verify it.

findings.title: Text S3 is cited for the OLS regression coefficients but contains only a one-sentence 'available upon request' data statement
findings.reported: "Both unstandardized ( B ) and standardized ( b ) OLS regression coefficients are reported (see Text S3)."
findings.computed: Text S3, read directly at this stage via extract_supplement, contains no regression output and no tables. Its complete contents are: "Text S3: Raw data are available upon request for replication purposes." The specification of the three life-satisfaction models -- which predictors were entered, in what order, with what standard errors and R-squared -- is therefore documented in neither the article nor any of the six supplements. Separately, "available upon request" is a state-but-withhold data declaration rather than actual availability.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. A late renumbering of the six supplementary files would be an innocent explanation for the broken pointer, but the Stage-1 sweep read all six and none contains regression output, so the material appears never to have been supplied rather than merely misnumbered.

consequence.explanation: The two life-satisfaction results, t(73) = -2.39 and t(72) = 2.34, cannot be independently reconstructed, because neither the model specification nor the underlying data is obtainable from the published record.

findings.plain: The paper tells readers that the details of its life-satisfaction analysis -- the second of its two main results -- are in a supporting file. That file is one sentence long and says only that the raw data can be had on request. So the model behind one of the paper's two headline claims is written down nowhere, and the data that would let someone rebuild it is not actually posted. This does not mean the result is wrong; it means nobody outside the author team can check it.

findings.title: The life-satisfaction result (p = .02) does not survive correction for the family of tests the Results actually report
findings.reported: No correction for multiple comparisons is mentioned anywhere. "Significance testing of fixed effects was performed using chisquared distributed (df = 1) Wald-tests." The claim at issue: "satisfaction levels declined over time, B = 2 .012, b = 2 .124, t (73) = 2 2.39, p =.02".
findings.computed: Over the broad family of significance tests reported in the Results, 7 were evaluable after 8 threshold p-values were dropped; family-wise error rate up to 30.2%; Bonferroni threshold .0071. Of 2 results significant uncorrected, 0 survive under Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg or Benjamini-Yekutieli; n_claims_lost_to_correction = 2. Those two are the same cognitive outcome fitted with and without a loneliness covariate, so they represent one distinct claim. Re-run on the narrow family of just the two primary outcomes -- with the affective p recovered as 7.6e-08 by recalc_stat_to_p from the printed chi-square of 28.90 -- both survive every correction and n_claims_lost_to_correction = 0. The affective claim is untouched under any family: at p around 8e-08 it clears even a Bonferroni threshold over all 15 tests.
findings.assumptions: Family definition is my judgement and the caveat must travel with the number: the result flips entirely on it. I supplied two families and report both. The true comparison count exceeds 15, because roughly twelve moderation tests and two interaction tests are summarised only as 'ps > .16' and 'ps > .44' and two further tests sit in the supplements, so this is a floor on the multiplicity problem. Uncorrected testing was ordinary practice in 2013 experience-sampling work and this is not a claim that the authors departed from their field's norms; it is an arithmetic statement about what their numbers support.

consequence.explanation: The abstract's second claim -- that the more people used Facebook over two weeks, the more their life satisfaction declined -- crosses back above the alpha the paper used once the Results' own family of tests is corrected for, though it survives if only the two primary outcomes are counted as the family.

findings.plain: The paper runs at least fifteen statistical tests and adjusts for none of them. When many tests are run, some will look significant by luck alone, and the usual remedy is to demand a stricter standard of each. The paper's first main result -- that using Facebook predicts feeling worse shortly afterwards -- is so strong that no such adjustment touches it. The second -- that heavier Facebook use over two weeks predicts falling life satisfaction -- is borderline to begin with, and whether it holds up depends entirely on how many tests you consider it to belong with: counted against just the two headline analyses it survives comfortably, counted against everything reported in the Results it does not. That ambiguity is itself the finding, and it is the abstract's second sentence of results that hangs on it.

findings.title: Causal phrasing in the figure caption and Discussion contradicts the paper's own statement that causation is not established
findings.reported: Figure 1 caption: "Interacting with Facebook during one time period (Time1-2) leads people to feel worse later on during the same day (T2)". Discussion: "In fact, direct social network interactions led people to feel better over time." Against, in the same paper: "although the analytic approach we used in this study is useful for drawing inferences about the likely causal ordering of associations between naturally occurring variables, experiments that manipulate Facebook use in daily life are needed to corroborate these findings and establish definitive causal relations."
findings.computed: No computation. This is a reading of two passages of the same document that cannot both be taken at face value: the design is observational experience sampling with no manipulation of Facebook use, which the Future research section concedes, while the figure caption and one Discussion sentence use unhedged causal verbs. In fairness the title ("Facebook Use Predicts Declines..."), the abstract's results sentences and nearly all of the Results section use "predicts", which is the correct and careful form, so this is a localised lapse rather than the paper's general register.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The judgement that lagged observational data cannot license "leads to" is a standard inferential point and is also the paper's own stated position.
findings.reproduction: no command applies -- this is a comparison of two passages of the paper's prose, not an arithmetic result

consequence.explanation: Affects how the paper's central finding is read -- as an established cause or as a temporal association -- without changing any reported number.

findings.plain: The study watched people's ordinary Facebook use; it did not assign anyone to use Facebook more or less. The authors say so themselves, noting that experiments would be needed to establish cause. But the caption of their main figure says Facebook use "leads people to feel worse", and the discussion says direct social contact "led people to feel better" -- both of which assert cause. The title and nearly all of the results text are worded correctly, so this is a slip in two places rather than the tone of the whole paper; it matters because a figure caption is one of the most-quoted parts of a paper.

findings.title: Three of the four race/ethnicity percentages are unattainable as shares of the stated 82 participants
findings.reported: "Eighty-two people ( M age =19.52, SD age =2.17; 53 females; 60.5% European American, 28.4% Asian, 6.2% African American, and 4.9% other) were recruited for a study on Facebook through flyers posted around Ann Arbor, Michigan."
findings.computed: Sweeping every denominator from 2 to the paper's own stated total of 82: only 4.9% is attainable as a share of 82 (k=4). 60.5% is attainable only at n = 38, 43, 76 or 81; 28.4% only at n = 67, 74 or 81; 6.2% at n = 16, 32, 48, 64, 65, 80 or 81. The unique denominator satisfying all four simultaneously is 81, giving counts 49 + 23 + 5 + 4 = 81. Against this, three other statistics in the same Methods section -- mean age 19.52, BDI mean 9.02 and Rosenberg mean 30.40 -- all pass GRIM cleanly at n = 82, which argues against 82 being simply a wrong total.
findings.assumptions: The search ceiling is the paper's OWN stated n of 82, so the exclusion of 82 is a fact about the paper rather than about a range I chose. The GRIM checks at n=82 assume age was recorded in whole years (assumed) and that BDI and Rosenberg totals are integer sums (which they are by construction).

consequence.explanation: Sample-composition reporting only; no inferential claim in the paper depends on the race/ethnicity breakdown.

findings.plain: The paper says 82 people took part and gives their ethnic breakdown as 60.5%, 28.4%, 6.2% and 4.9%. Three of those four figures cannot be produced by any whole number of people out of 82 -- but all four fit exactly out of 81 people (49, 23, 5 and 4). The most likely explanation is entirely innocent: one participant probably did not report their ethnicity, so the percentages were worked out over the 81 who did. The paper never says so, and no note about missing data appears anywhere. Nothing the paper concludes depends on these figures.

findings.title: A t statistic is printed positive while both coefficients on the same line are negative
findings.reported: "''direct'' social interaction did not predict changes in cognitive well-being, B = 2 .006, b = 2 .059, t (73) = 1.04, p =.30"
findings.computed: A t statistic carries the sign of the coefficient it tests. Both coefficients on this line are negative and the t is printed positive. In this PDF's text layer the minus sign renders as the digit 2, and it appears before .006 and .059 but not before 1.04; the parallel sentence on the preceding page prints it consistently -- "B = 2 .012, b = 2 .124, t (73) = 2 2.39" -- so the asymmetry is in the source rather than introduced by extraction. Independently verified that |t| = 1.04 at df = 73 gives p = .3018, matching the printed .30 exactly, so the arithmetic is untouched.
findings.assumptions: Rests on this PDF's text layer, in which minus renders as '2' throughout. A reader looking at the typeset page should confirm the sign directly. Almost certainly a typesetting or transcription slip rather than anything substantive.

consequence.explanation: The sign of the t changes neither the p-value nor the null conclusion drawn from it.

findings.plain: On one line the paper reports two negative numbers and then a test statistic that should carry the same minus sign but is printed without it. This is almost certainly a typographical slip: the result is the same either way, and the accompanying p-value of .30 checks out exactly. Recorded only because the sentence supports a claim that appears in the abstract, so the line is worth getting right.

findings.title: The number of participants in the life-satisfaction models and Table 1 is never stated
findings.location: Results, Attrition and compliance; Results, Cognitive well-being; Table 1
findings.reported: "Three participants did not complete the study... we pruned the data by excluding all of the data from two participants who responded to , 33% of the texts, resulting in 4,589 total observations." Table 1 states no sample size for either its within-person or its between-person half.
findings.computed: The observation count (4,589) is given but the participant-level analytic n appears in zero places. The only trace of it is the residual degrees-of-freedom chain across the three OLS models -- 73 with 3 predictors, 72 with 4, 71 with 5 -- which steps down by exactly one per added covariate, an internally coherent pattern implying about 77 participants. That inference, not a stated figure, is what every participant-level check in this review had to use.
findings.assumptions: The step of exactly one df per added covariate is the paper's own pattern, not an assumption I supplied. I did not treat 77 as established, and labelled it an inference wherever it was used.
findings.reproduction: no command applies -- this records a value the paper never prints, not an arithmetic result

consequence.explanation: Table 1's correlations, the twelve moderation tests and all three life-satisfaction models rest on a sample size the reader is never told, so their precision cannot be independently judged.

findings.plain: The paper says 82 people were recruited, three dropped out and two more were removed, but it never states how many people ended up in the main life-satisfaction analysis or in its correlation table. A reader has to work it out backwards from a technical by-product of the analysis, which points to about 77. The figure is missing rather than wrong -- the internal bookkeeping is consistent -- but it means the precision of the correlation table cannot be checked at all.

findings.title: A standardized coefficient of .129 carries t = 0.39 while one of -.124 carries t = -2.39, with no standard errors reported to reconcile them
findings.location: Results, Exploratory analyses vs Results, Cognitive well-being
findings.computed: Two standardized coefficients of near-equal magnitude (.129 and -.124) are reported with markedly different test statistics (0.39 and -2.39) in models fitted to the same participants. No computation adjudicates this, because the standard errors that would are not reported. There is an entirely ordinary explanation and it is probably the right one: the second model adds an apparently uncentred Facebook-use by direct-contact product term, and the resulting collinearity inflates the standard error of every term involving it, which is exactly how a sizeable standardized coefficient ends up with a small test statistic.
findings.assumptions: I did not derive the standard errors from the coefficients and test statistics; that would have been unguarded arithmetic. Without them the collinearity explanation cannot be distinguished from a transcription error in the coefficient, so no flag is raised.
findings.reproduction: no command applies -- this is a comparison of printed coefficients across two models, and the standard errors needed to adjudicate it are not published

consequence.explanation: Concerns an analysis the paper itself labels exploratory and draws no conclusion from; recorded because it is where the missing supplement has its most concrete cost.

findings.plain: In one analysis the paper reports an effect of a certain size that is statistically significant; in another, on the same people, it reports an effect of almost exactly the same size that is not remotely significant. There is a routine technical reason why that can happen legitimately, and it is probably what happened here. But confirming it requires a number -- the margin of error on each estimate -- that the paper does not publish anywhere, which is the same gap left by the missing supplementary file. So this cannot be resolved either way, and it is recorded as unresolved rather than as a problem.

findings.title: No sample-size justification or power analysis is reported, and the null moderation claims are where that matters
findings.reported: "Eighty-two people... were recruited for a study on Facebook through flyers posted around Ann Arbor, Michigan." No target sample size, alpha, target power or expected effect size is stated.
findings.computed: verify_power_analysis was the appropriate check and could not be run: it requires a stated effect size, alpha and target power, and the paper states none of the three. Recorded as a refusal rather than a substituted calculation.
findings.assumptions: Explicitly contextual: an a-priori power analysis was not standard practice for experience-sampling research in 2013 and this is NOT offered as a criticism of the authors' conduct. It is recorded only because it bears on the moderation nulls in finding 1 -- the participant-level tests run on roughly 77 people, and the authors themselves describe their effects as 'small'.
findings.reproduction: no command applies -- a power check requires a stated effect size, alpha and target power, and the paper states none of them

consequence.explanation: Bears on how much weight the twelve null moderation results can carry, not on any positive finding.

findings.plain: The paper does not explain why 82 people were recruited, or how large an effect that number of people could reliably detect. For a study of this type published in 2013 that is completely ordinary and is not a criticism. It is noted only because the paper makes several claims that something was NOT found, and how much those claims are worth depends on how good the study was at finding things -- which, with roughly 77 people and effects the authors themselves call small, was probably not very.

triage.reason: Folded into finding 1 with text_s6_cited_for_moderation_contains_no_moderation_results: the broken cross-reference and the unbounded null claim are one underlying problem -- the moderation analyses are undocumented -- and splitting them would double-count a single defect.

The tool refused rather than flagged: at n=82 with a 2-decimal mean every value failing round-half passes under truncation, so the check has no discriminating power and the result is evidence of nothing.

Kept at suspicious but confidence lowered to medium and consequence set to zero claims: it rests on a text layer in which minus renders as '2', and is a typesetting slip that leaves the p-value and the conclusion unchanged.

Re-run at stage 2 on two families rather than one; the narrow two-primary-outcome family loses 0 claims, so the finding is now reported as conditional on family definition rather than as a flat loss of two claims.
The tool returned consistent -- the achievable p interval for r = .22 spans .05 at the inferred n of 77, so the asterisk cannot be contradicted and there is no finding to carry.

not_checked.reason: Both panels are path diagrams annotated with regression weights. The two weights named in the caption's prose were verified against the Results text, but the diagrams very likely also print the autoregressive paths (T1 affect to T2 affect; pre to post life satisfaction) and possibly significance stars, and those coefficients appear nowhere in the text or in Table 1. Figure extraction was not run, so any value carried only by the figure is unchecked.

The table states no sample size for either its within-person or its between-person half, and no n for it appears anywhere in the paper. Significance is shown only as asterisk thresholds with no exact p-values. Only the single borderline cell (r = .22*) was close enough to .05 to be testable, and it was consistent at the df-implied n of 77.

not_checked.location: Results, Moderation -- roughly twelve moderator tests summarised as 'ps > .16'
not_checked.reason: No coefficient, standard error, test statistic, exact p or confidence interval is reported for any individual moderation test, in the article or in any of the six supplements. Nothing can be recomputed and no interval can be bounded. This is finding 1.

not_checked.location: Results, Alternative explanations -- worry and loneliness interactions summarised as 'ps > .44'
not_checked.reason: Reported only as a minimum p across two interaction tests, with no statistics attached to either.

Deliberately not run. This PDF's font encoding renders every minus sign as the digit 2 and every chi-square as 'x2', so 't(73) = -2.39' appears in the text layer as 't (73) = 2 2.39'. Feeding that to statcheck would report inconsistencies that are artefacts of extraction rather than properties of the paper. Instead all 17 test statistics were verified individually with recalc_stat_to_p, so coverage of the NHST statistics is complete; only the automated scanner was skipped.

not_checked.location: Compliance arithmetic: 83.6% mean response rate, range 18.6%-100%, and 4,589 total observations
not_checked.reason: These can only be reconciled by choosing a denominator the paper does not state -- whether the 83.6% mean was taken over 79 completers or all 82 recruited, and whether the maximum per participant was 70 signals. No check applies without inventing that denominator.

not_checked.location: SD plausibility for the five experience-sampled slider items
not_checked.reason: check_sd_range is CLI-only and not callable from the sweep stage. In any case all five SDs sit far below the range/2 ceiling of 50 imposed by the stated 0-100 bounds, so no violation is possible and the check would add nothing.
Not applicable. The paper contains exactly one table and it is a correlation matrix, not a table of means and SDs, so there is no second block of summary statistics to compare it against.

Deliberately not run. The effects are small (standardized coefficient -.124 for the life-satisfaction outcome), which is typical for social-psychological field data, and the authors themselves flag them as 'small'. There is no implausibly large effect for this check to adjudicate.

not_checked.location: GRIM on the SWLS, Social Provision Scale and UCLA Loneliness means
not_checked.reason: All three are means of multi-item composites, so their granularity is finer than the second decimal place at roughly 80 participants. GRIM has no discriminating power here and would manufacture false reassurance rather than evidence.

limitations: This agent reads text and does not see figures. Figure extraction was NOT run on this paper, so nothing in Figure 1's two path diagrams was read; the autoregressive coefficients those panels almost certainly print appear nowhere in the text or Table 1 and are entirely unchecked.

Two of the findings rest on what supplementary files do NOT contain. I did not inherit that from the sweep: I read Text S3 and Text S6 directly at this stage and quote their complete contents. The claim that none of the other four supplements contains regression or moderation output rests on the Stage-1 sweep's reads, which I did not repeat.

All six accusations arrived flagged as 'quote not located'. I re-read the full body text at this stage and located every one of the six quotes verbatim, so the flags were a failure of our own quote-matching -- probably typographic normalisation -- and not of the evidence. None was dropped on that basis.

The participant-level sample size of 77 used throughout is an inference from the paper's residual degrees of freedom, not a stated figure. Every check that depended on it is correspondingly conditional, and the borderline Table 1 correlation would be comfortably significant at any larger n.

The multiplicity result flips on how the family of tests is defined, which is a judgement no tool can make. Both a broad and a narrow family were computed and both are reported; a reader who considers only the two primary outcomes to be the family will correctly conclude that nothing is lost to correction.

This system reads one paper and reaches no network. It cannot say whether similar reporting patterns appear in other work by these authors, nor how this paper's effect sizes compare with others in the same literature -- both of which are relevant to a paper whose findings have been extensively re-examined since 2013, and neither of which is settled here.

This PDF's font encoding renders minus signs as the digit 2, which is why the sign-notation finding carries only medium confidence; a reader with the typeset page in front of them can settle it in seconds.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods state that "Both unstandardized (B) and standardized (b) OLS regression coefficients are reported (see Text S3)", but Text S3 as published reads in full: "Raw data are available upon request for replication purposes." Could you send the regression output for the three life-satisfaction models -- the predictors entered, coefficients, standard errors and R-squared for the models with 73, 72 and 71 residual degrees of freedom?
questions_for_authors.why: Would settle finding 2 and allow the paper's second headline claim to be reconstructed; the standard errors would also resolve finding 8.

questions_for_authors.question: The Moderation section summarises tests of roughly twelve moderators as "In no case did we observe any significant interactions (ps > .16)", and the abstract states that the effects were "not moderated by" seven of them. Could you send the coefficient, standard error and exact p-value for each individual moderation test?
questions_for_authors.why: Would settle finding 1 and allow the largest moderating effect still compatible with the data to be bounded, which cannot currently be done from anything published.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods report 82 participants with a race/ethnicity breakdown of 60.5%, 28.4%, 6.2% and 4.9%. Of these, only 4.9% is attainable as a whole-participant share of 82, whereas all four are attainable at 81 (49, 23, 5 and 4 participants). Was race/ethnicity unrecorded for one participant, so that the percentages were computed over 81?
questions_for_authors.why: Would settle finding 5 and confirm whether 82 is the correct recruited total, which three other Methods statistics support.

questions_for_authors.question: The paper reports 4,589 observations but does not state the participant-level sample size for the OLS life-satisfaction models or for the Table 1 correlations; the residual degrees of freedom imply 77. Could you confirm the number of participants in each of those analyses?
questions_for_authors.why: Would settle finding 7 and fix the denominator for Table 1, whose 31 correlations currently cannot be checked against any stated n.

questions_for_authors.question: In "''direct'' social interaction did not predict changes in cognitive well-being, B = -.006, b = -.059, t(73) = 1.04, p = .30", the t is printed positive while both coefficients are negative, unlike the parallel line on the previous page which reads "t(73) = -2.39". Should the t read -1.04?
questions_for_authors.why: Would settle finding 6, a probable typesetting slip on a line supporting an abstract-level claim.

input.report_markdown:
This paper text-messaged 82 young adults five times a day for fourteen days, asking each time how they felt and how much they had used Facebook since the previous message, and bracketed the fortnight with a life-satisfaction questionnaire. It reports two findings: that Facebook use at one moment predicts feeling worse at the next, and that heavier Facebook use across the fortnight predicts declining life satisfaction. It further reports that face-to-face contact did the opposite, and that neither effect was moderated by seven individual-difference variables.

The arithmetic in this paper is clean, and that deserves saying first and plainly. All seventeen test statistics reported in the article and its supplements were converted to p-values individually, and every one reconciles with the p-value printed beside it -- including the close calls, which are reported in the direction that works against the authors rather than for them. A chi-square of 10.78 gives p = .00103, and the authors wrote "p < .01" where "p < .001" would have looked stronger and been wrong by a hair. A chi-square of 11.21 gives p = .00081, and "p < .001" is correct. Three of the four Methods means (age, Beck Depression Inventory, Rosenberg Self-Esteem) pass granularity checks at the stated sample size, and the ethnicity percentages sum exactly to 100. Twenty-three of the thirty-three checks that could be run came back consistent, four were refused by our own tools for want of an input, and six were flagged. Nothing in this paper is arithmetically impossible, and no check produced a value that could not have come from real data.

The problems are of a different kind entirely: they concern what a reader is permitted to verify.

Two supplementary files are cited for material they do not contain, and I read both directly rather than taking the sweep's word for it. Text S3, cited in the Methods as the source of the OLS regression coefficients, is one sentence saying the raw data are available on request. Text S6, cited at the sentence summarising twelve moderation tests, is one sentence explaining why a thirteenth variable was not tested. Between them these two pointers account for the model specification behind one headline claim and the entire evidential basis of an abstract-level claim, and neither is documented anywhere in the published record. The "available upon request" formulation compounds the first: it is a statement about availability rather than availability itself.

On multiplicity I want to be careful, because the answer depends on a judgement the arithmetic cannot make. Fifteen significance tests are reported with no correction of any kind, which was ordinary practice for this literature in 2013 and is not a departure from anything the authors claimed. What the arithmetic does say is that the paper's two headline claims are in very different positions. The affective result is enormous by the standards of correction -- its true p is around eight in a hundred million, and it clears any threshold one might impose over any family one might define. The life-satisfaction result sits at p = .02, and whether it survives depends entirely on the company it keeps: counted against only the two primary outcomes it survives every correction with room to spare; counted against the tests the Results section actually reports, it survives none of them. Both computations are in the findings. A reader should know that the paper's first claim is robust here and its second is not, and that the second is the one the abstract states in its most quotable form.

Two smaller observations round this out. The race/ethnicity percentages fit 81 participants exactly and fit 82 only in one of four cases -- almost certainly one unrecorded response rather than anything else, but the paper carries no missing-data note, and three other statistics in the same paragraph do fit 82. And the figure caption asserts that Facebook use "leads people to feel worse", which the paper's own Future research section concedes this design cannot establish; the title and nearly all of the Results are worded correctly as "predicts", so this is a lapse in two places rather than the paper's habitual register.

What this analysis cannot do is reach outside the document. Whether reporting of this kind is characteristic of these authors, and how these effect sizes sit against the wider literature on social media and well-being -- a literature that has grown considerably since 2013 and has revisited this specific question repeatedly -- are questions a reader must answer elsewhere. They are not answered here.

The numbers this paper prints are consistent with each other and with the tests they are attached to. What cannot be checked is a good deal of what the paper asserts: the model behind its life-satisfaction claim, and every one of the twelve moderation tests underwriting a sentence in its abstract. I would treat the first headline finding as well supported by what is printed, the second as fragile and unreconstructible, and the abstract's no-moderation claim as unsupported by anything a reader can inspect.
